## Methods

Materials
Zn(CF3SO3)2 (purity ≥99.5%) was purchased from Duoduo Chem. ZnSO4·7H2O (purity ≥99%), ZnCl2 (purity ≥99.99% metals basis), Zn(ClO4)2·6H2O (purity ≥99.995% metals basis), Na2SO4 (purity ≥99%), NaI (purity ≥99.5%), ZnI2 (purity ≥98%), I2 (purity ≥99.8%), ethanol (purity ≥99.5%), Acetylcholine bromide (purity ≥98%), Acetylcholine chloride (purity ≥99%), and Acetylthiocholine iodide (purity ≥98%) were procured from Aladdin. Choline iodide (purity ≥98%) and Butyrylcholine iodide (purity ≥99%) were bought from Macklin. Acetylcholine iodide (purity >98%) were obtained from TCI. Activated carbon (AC, YP50F) and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE, PTFE-770) was purchased from Shenzhen Kejing Star Technology Co., Ltd. Zn foil (purity ≥99.99%), Ti foil (purity ≥99.99%), Zn wire (purity ≥99.99%) and Ti wire (purity ≥99.99%) were purchased from Wuhan Luojia Yanxin Technology Co., Ltd.

Electrolyte preparation
For the 1 M ZnOTF electrolyte, 36.353 g Zinc trifluoromethanesulfonate was completely dissolved in ultrapure water to form a 100 mL solution with a volumetric flask. The ZnOTF-ACI electrolyte was prepared similarly, except that a certain amount of acetylcholine iodide powder was introduced during dissolution. The electrolyte preparation was conducted in an ambient atmosphere at 25±2°C. Our experiments indicate that the optimum concentration of ACI is ~0.5 M (Supplementary Fig. 36).

Electrode fabrication
AC electrode. The AC electrode was prepared by a dry process. AC powder and PTFE powder were manually mixed at a 9:1 weight ratio until uniform, then transferred to the chamber of a high-speed disperser (MSK-SFM-D300, Shenzhen Kejing Star Technology Co., Ltd). After rotating at 9000 rpm for 4 min and repeating this process three times, the PTFE powder transformed into fibers and created a robust network to bind the AC powder. The mixture was then evenly spread onto a cleaned aluminium foil and converted into a seamless, self-supporting film by a hot calendering machine (MSK-H2150-E, Shenzhen Kejing Star Technology Co., Ltd) at 60±2°C. The thickness of the AC film was controlled by adjusting the gap between the two rolls of the calendering machine. By sandwiching a titanium mesh collector between two AC films and consolidating them using a mechanical press (PC-30, Tianjin Jingtuo Instrument Technology Co., Ltd), the AC electrodes were obtained. They were then resized according to the requirements of the different cells.

I2 positive electrode. The aforementioned AC electrode was used as the host for the I2 to produce a composite electrode. A low-loaded I2 positive electrode (~5.3 mg cm−2, for a coin cell) was prepared by a drop-coating method, which involved dropping an appropriate amount of I2 containing ethanol solution onto a thin AC electrode (~6 mg cm−2). High-loaded I2 positive electrodes (~28 and ~84 mg cm−2) were prepared by electrodepositing. Specifically, thick AC electrodes and Zn foils were used as the positive and negative electrodes, respectively. These electrodes were placed on opposite sides of an acrylic container, with a 0.5 M ZnI2 aqueous electrolyte filling the space between them. During galvanostatic charging, iodine ions in the electrolyte were electroplated onto the AC electrodes to form solid I2. An areal iodine loading of ~28 mg cm−2 was achieved by charging at a current density of 150 mA for 2 h on a 7×7 cm2 AC electrode. A higher loading of ~84 mg cm−2 (for the bi-layer pouch cells) was achieved by charging at 600 mA for 2 h on a 7.5×9.5 cm2 AC electrode. The iodine positive electrode was obtained by washing several times with ultrapure water and drying for 24 h in an oven at 40°C.

Pouch cell assembly
Zn foils were mechanically polished and rinsed in ethanol before use. The Zn||Zn pouch cell was assembled using two polished Zn foils (7×7 cm2) and one Whatman GF/B glass fiber separator (7.2×7.2 cm2), with 5 mL of electrolyte injected. The thickness of the Whatman GF/B separator after compression is ~500 μm, with an average pore size of 1.0 μm. For a single-layer pouch cell, one I2 positive electrode (7×7 cm2) and one Zn negative electrode (7×7 cm2) were placed on either side of the separator. An Ah-scale Zn||I2 pouch cell was produced by a bi-layer structure of two Zn negative electrodes (7.5×9.5 cm2), one I2 positive electrode (7.5×9.5 cm2), and two separators (7.7×9.7 cm2). These assembled stacks were accommodated in Al-plastic bag and filled with electrolyte. The injection of the electrolyte for single-layer Zn-I2 pouch cells and Ah-scale Zn||I2 pouch cells was controlled at approximately 21 and 10 μL mAh−1, respectively. After degassing and heat sealing, these pouch cells rested for 2 h to ensure complete wetting. Galvanostatic cycling stability tests were conducted under a uniform pressure (~2 kPa) to ensure satisfactory component contact for these cells.

Material characterization
The morphologies, microstructure, and corresponding elemental maps were obtained using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Thermo Scientific Apreo 2S) equipped with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). The crystallographic phase and chemical composition were analyzed by (XRD, Rigaku MiniFlex), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, PHI 5000 Versa Probe II), and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES, Arcos II MV). The surface roughness and 3D morphologies of Zn negative electrodes were examined using the same 3D microscope. The cycled Zn electrode is extracted from the cell and cleaned with ultrapure water and ethanol. Following vacuum drying at 40°C for 2 h, it is subjected to SEM, XRD, and other tests. The UV/Vis absorption spectra of iodine-containing solutions were tested by a UV/Vis spectrometer (LAMBDA 365) after diluting with ultrapure water by a factor of 50.

In situ optical observation
The optical microscopy observations were conducted using a home-made liquid cell, where a Ti wire (30 mm in length and 0.5 mm in diameter), a Zn wire (30 mm in length and 1 mm in diameter), and a Zn wire (10 mm in length and 1 mm in diameter) served as the working, counter, and reference electrodes, respectively. Prior to the assembly of the optical cell, the Ti wire and Zn wire were polished with 10,000 mesh sandpaper to remove surface oxides and thoroughly cleaned with deionized water and ethanol. The cell was sealed with waterproof tape to prevent electrolyte leakage. The optical cell was connected to a battery tester to perform a cycle of Zn plating and stripping. Corresponding voltage response was also recorded. Meanwhile, an ultra-depth three-dimensional microscope (DeltaPix DPXM6000) was used to capture a series of changes in Zn plating/stripping morphology over time during the cycle.

In situ EQCM
In situ EQCM (DyneChem DC-QMC3100) measurements were performed in a three-electrode cell consisting of an Au wafer working electrode, Ti counter electrode, and Ag/AgCl reference electrode. The assembled cell was examined with a LSV test at 5 mV s−1. The change in resonant frequency (Δf) of the quartz crystal during the LSV test was recorded. Therefore, the mass change (Δm) of the quartz crystal electrode can be calculated using the following Sauerbrey equation:
Δm = −(C × A × sqrt(ρμ) × Δf) / (2f0^2) (1)
Where A is the piezoelectrically active crystal area (0.28274 cm2), ρ is the density of quartz (2.648 g cm−3), μ is the shear modulus of quartz (2.947×1011 g cm−1 s−2), f0 is the resonant frequency of the quartz crystal (9 MHz), and Δf is the frequency change.

In situ FT-IR
In situ FT-IR measurements were performed using a ThermoFisher Scientific Nicolet iS50 spectrometer equipped with a liquid nitrogen-cooled Mercury Cadmium Telluride (MCT) detector and a silicon attenuated total reflection (ATR) accessory. Prior to use, the substrate plane of the Si prism was mechanically polished using aluminum oxide suspensions of different particle sizes until a mirror-like finish was achieved, followed by rinsing with deionized water. In the in situ FTIR cell, a Ti mesh served as the working electrode, while Zn foil functioned as both the counter electrode and reference electrode. The incidence angle was set at 60°, with a spectral resolution of 4 cm−1. Each spectral data was collected at an interval of 60 s. The FT-IR spectroscopy combined with the galvanostatic discharge method was used to monitor the Zn deposition process on the electrode surface.

Electrochemical measurements
The Zn||Zn symmetrical coin cells (CR2032) were assembled with two identical polished Zn foils (~45 μm in thickness and 12 mm in diameter), one Whatman GF/B glass fiber separator (16 mm in diameter), and 120 μL of the electrolyte. Galvanostatic Zn plating/stripping was performed in different cycling conditions. For Zn||Ti asymmetrical coin cells, Ti foil (~30 μm in thickness and 12 mm in diameter) was used as the working electrode, and the charge cutoff potential was set at 0.5 V (vs. Zn/Zn2+). A “reservoir” protocol was used to assess the average CE of Zn plating/stripping. First, the assembled asymmetrical Zn-Ti cell was subjected to one cycle at a capacity of 5 mAh cm−2 to remove any impurities on the Ti substrate. Then, a given amount of charge (QT), e.g., 5 mAh cm−2, was deposited on the Ti substrate as a Zn “reservoir”. Afterwards, repeated Zn stripping/plating was conducted (10 cycles) under a areal capacity (QC) of 1 mAh cm−2. Finally, the residual Zn was completely stripped at a cut-off potential of 0.5 V (vs. Zn/Zn2+), providing the final stripping capacity (QS). The average CE was calculated using the following equation:
CEavg = (QS + 10 × QC) / (QT + 10 × QC) (2)
The voltage window for the Zn||I2 cells was 0.3–1.8 V. The hydrogen evolution performance was investigated in a 1 M Na2SO4 aqueous solution with a three-electrode system using Zn deposits as the working electrode, platinum as the counter electrode, and Ag/AgCl as the reference electrode. In situ EIS was conducted every 10 min during Zn plating using an electrochemical workstation (Biologic VSP-3e). The EIS spectra were collected over the frequency range of 105 to 0.05 Hz under open-circuit potential conditions with a potentiostatic mode (10 mV amplitude, 10 points per decade). For resistivity tests, the voltage response was measured at a constant current of 0.5 mA on a sample sandwiched between two stainless steel electrodes. The resistivity (ρ) was calculated using the following equation:
ρ = (U × S) / (I × L) (3)
where U is the average response voltage, S is the contact area (1.13 cm2), I is the applied current (0.5 mA), and L is the thickness of the sample (~45 μm). The electrochemical experiments were conducted in an air-conditioned laboratory environment with an average temperature of 25 ± 2°C.

Finite element simulations
Finite element method simulations were performed using COMSOL Multiphysics. A two-dimensional model was developed to simulate the current density and electric field distribution at the negative electrode/electrolyte interface. In this model, the length of two electrodes was 15 μm and the distance between them was 10 μm. The lumpy Zn was represented by three hexagonal protrusions, each with a side length of 2 μm. Additionally, rectangular Zn with a height of 1 μm and width of 0.1 μm were incorporated on the hexagons to simulate mossy Zn growth. The ionic conductivity of the 1 M ZnOTF electrolyte filling the interelectrode gap was set to 3.2 S m−159. The positive electrode and negative electrode potentials were held at 0.05 and 0 V (vs. Zn/Zn2+), respectively.

DFT calculations
First-principles DFT calculations were performed in the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP)60. The exchange-correlation interactions were described by the PBE functional within the generalized gradient approximation, with a plane-wave cutoff energy of 500 eV61. The electronic self-consistency criterion was set to 10−5 eV, and the force on each atom was converged below 0.03 eV Å−1. The Zn substrate was modeled as a four-layer 6×6 supercell and a 25 Å vacuum layer was constructed. The dispersion corrections were included by the DFT-D3 scheme. Geometry optimizations were performed using a Γ-only k-mesh for the Brillouin zone sampling. The geometry relaxation was applied for the top two layers of the Zn slab62. The adsorption energy (Eads) was calculated using the following equation:
Eads = Etotal − Esub − EZn (4)
where Etotal is the total energy of the adsorption system, Esub is the total energy of the adsorbate, EZn is the energy of a free Zn(002)-slab.

Data availability
All data generated in this study are provided in the manuscript, Supplementary Information, and Source Data file. Source data are provided with this paper.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This study provides an interesting discovery of two-stage Zn deposition and proposes an effective anion-cation additive (ACI) to suppress mossy Zn formation and revive dead Zn. The Zn anodes exhibited considerable advances in compact deposition and cycling performance. And the practical applications have also been well demonstrated in Ah-scale pouch cells. These results would be of general interest to the relevant research field. Therefore, this manuscript is suitable for publication in Nature Communications after addressing the following concerns.
1. Regarding the in-situ optical observation of two-stage Zn deposition, I am curious why the authors used a Ti wire electrode as the working electrode. Does this two-stage deposition phenomenon also exist in conventional planar electrodes and batteries? Additional experiments are needed to strengthen the universality of two-stage deposition.
2. As we all known, the shuttle effect in zinc-iodine batteries involves polyiodide species (e.g., I3−, I5−) migrating to the negative electrode, causing capacity decay and Zn corrosion. Here, the author proposes that the oxidative I3− reacts with dead zinc to increase the reversibility of the Zn anode. Could this process exacerbate Zn corrosion? An explanation is needed for why I₃⁻ does not intensify side reactions.
3. In Fig. 3a, EQCM data show mass changes but cannot distinguish between cation adsorption and cation-anion co-adsorption. Control experiments testing the anion alone (e.g., iodide salts without acetylcholine) would clarify interfacial interactions.
4. Could the iodine anion independently affect the morphology of zinc deposits? Please provide more experiments and explanations.
5. Is ACI’s success specific to the ZnOTF electrolyte? Testing ACI with alternative zinc salts (e.g., ZnSO4) would demonstrate broader applicability.
6. In Fig.6, an activation process is observed in Zn||I₂ pouch cells with ACI but not in coin cells. Please give an explanation.
7. In Zn||Zn symmetric cell testing, the overpotential of the ZnOTF-ACI electrolyte gradually increases upon cycling. What causes this?
8. A thorough revision of the entire manuscript is recommended to correct some typos. For example, “0.2 Na2SO4” → “0.2 M Na2SO4” (Line 161), “whereases” → “whereas” (Line 191).

### Reviewer 2

This work investigates the failure mechanism of the Zn anode during cycling and reveals two distinct Zn deposition morphologies, which are critical to understanding the reversibility and cycling life of zinc-based batteries. Based on insights into the Zn deposition process, the authors design a bifunctional electrolyte additive that not only homogenizes Zn²⁺ flux but also facilitates the rejuvenation of inactive Zn via a spontaneous redox reaction. Benefiting from the engineered electrolyte, the authors demonstrate a significant enhancement in the lifespan of pouch cells. The bi-layer pouch cell shows promising practical performance under harsh testing conditions.
Overall, this study presents a comprehensive investigation, spanning from fundamental mechanism elucidation to material-level innovations and practical cell demonstrations. The experiments are thorough, and the research logic is generally sound. However, several minor issues remain, such as insufficient experimental details and ambiguous mechanistic explanations. Therefore, I recommend minor revision before the manuscript can be considered for publication in Nature Communications.
Comments and Suggestions:
1. Please provide a detailed schematic or image of the custom-designed three-electrode cell, preferably with multi-angle views and a magnified image of the central region. Additionally, the authors should explain why the deposited Zn appears luminescent. More experimental details regarding the custom-built optical microscope and EQCM setup are also needed.
2. There are some writing issues. For example, “0.2 Na₂SO₄” should be corrected to “0.2 M Na₂SO₄” or “0.2 mol L⁻¹ Na₂SO₄.”
3. The manuscript reports two Zn deposition morphologies: lumpy and mossy. The authors should provide a more in-depth analysis of the mechanisms driving these morphological differences. Is the variation substrate-induced, or does it relate to Zn²⁺ depletion near the electrode–electrolyte interface? The proposed mechanism, wherein edge growth of lumpy Zn disrupts the homogeneous Zn²⁺ flux, requires further clarification and supporting evidence.
4. In Figure 6a, the authors attribute the increase in capacity at higher current rates to redox activity of ACI. This interpretation is questionable without normalization to electrode mass or active material content. Please clarify.
5. In Figures 6c and 6d, the definition of C-rate appears inconsistent between the two cells. The authors should ensure consistent and clearly defined electrochemical testing parameters across figures.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript demonstrated the effect of bi-ionic effect of cation and anion on regulating Zn deposit morphology and reviving dead Zn via in situ optic microscopy. For confirming this effect, the authors showed a practical ampere hour scale pouch cell which has cycle retention of 96.2% for 800 cycles. However, this manuscript is not suitable for publication in Nature Communications due to its lack of novelty and insufficient depth in conveying a significant scientific message. Overall, the novelty and clarity of the proposed ACI mechanism are insufficient. To substantiate the hypothesis, further investigations using complementary analytical techniques or simulations are necessary.
The following comments are the reason why this manuscript is not suitable for publications.
1.The authors claim that the two-stage plating and stripping behavior of the Zn anode occurs only under their optical cell setup. However, in practical systems, Zn metal operates under applied pressure, and similar behaviors should also be examined in pressure-applied configurations, such as coin cells or pouch cells, at defined pressure levels. In addition, the plating and stripping behavior should be investigated using ZnSO₄ and other types of Zn salts to confirm whether the phenomenon is salt-dependent
2.The authors used Zn(OTf)2, which is significantly more expensive than ZnSO4. Since ZnSO4 is more widely used in practice, it is necessary for the authors to verify whether the two-stage plating and stripping behavior is also observed with other common Zn salts, such as ZnSO4, ZnCl2, and Zn(ClO4)2.
3.To ensure reliability, the influence of the bionic (ACI) effect on cell performance should be validated using other types of Zn salts
4.The overall analysis of the effect of ACI is insufficient to clearly elucidate the underlying mechanism. The mechanism of ACI is unclear for stabilizing the Zn metal interface.
5.There is no guarantee that iodine ions selectively decompose only ZOTH; they may also dissolve fresh Zn. Therefore, it is necessary to compare the decomposition ratio between fresh Zn and ZOTH. Furthermore, the adsorption selectivity of ZOTH to fresh Zn and dead Zn need to be analyzed.
6.Significantly, the effect of bi-ionic (ACI) should be more deeply studied with the mechanism and other types of bi-ionic form analogues should be compared.

Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable question. The observed activation
process (gradual capacity increase in the initial cycles) in the pouch cells is a common
characteristic of thick, high-loading electrodes and is not typically seen in thin-
electrode coin cells. This difference arises from the distinct electrode thickness and
mass loading used in the two cell configurations. Specifically, for coin cell tests, we
used thin electrodes with a moderate iodine loading of ~5 mg cm⁻² and a thickness of
~120 μm. At this scale, the electrode was readily wetted by the electrolyte. Therefore,
the cell achieved its maximum capacity almost immediately, with no significant
activation process. In contrast, practical pouch cells were assembled with thick, high-
loading electrodes (single-sided loading of ~28 mg cm⁻², thickness ~500 μm). This
dense, thick structure requires several cycles for the electrolyte to fully wet the
electrode and for the active material to be completely utilized. The gradual increase in
capacity during the initial cycles represents this progressive wetting and activation
process, which has been commonly reported in previous studies using similarly
designed thick electrodes (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 2024, 63: e202407909; Nat.
Commun., 2025, 16: 71).

This work investigates the failure mechanism of the Zn anode during cycling and
reveals two distinct Zn deposition morphologies, which are critical to understanding
the reversibility and cycling life of zinc-based batteries. Based on insights into the Zn
deposition process, the authors design a bifunctional electrolyte additive that not only
homogenizes Zn²⁺ flux but also facilitates the rejuvenation of inactive Zn via a
spontaneous redox reaction. Benefiting from the engineered electrolyte, the authors
demonstrate a significant enhancement in the lifespan of pouch cells. The bi-layer
pouch cell shows promising practical performance under harsh testing conditions.
Overall, this study presents a comprehensive investigation, spanning from
fundamental mechanism elucidation to material-level innovations and practical cell
demonstrations. The experiments are thorough, and the research logic is generally
sound. However, several minor issues remain, such as insufficient experimental
details and ambiguous mechanistic explanations. Therefore, I recommend minor
revision before the manuscript can be considered for publication in Nature
Communications.

Regarding to reviewer’s concern on the apparent luminescence of Zn deposits, this
phenomenon is primarily related to optical effects associated with surface topography
and light reflection. Specifically, the initially plated lumpy Zn are relatively dense and
compact with well-defined crystalline facets (as seen in Fig. 1d). This smooth Zn
surface acts like a mirror, specularly reflecting a large amount of incident light from
the microscope’s illumination source directly back into the objective lens. This high

appearance. In contrast, the mossy Zn consists of a porous, high-surface-area network
of Zn filaments. This rough structure scatters and absorbs incident light much more
effectively. Rather than being reflected directly back to the lens, the light is diffused
in many directions. Consequently, much less light reaches the detector, resulting in a
dark appearance.

Finally, after ruling out these potential reasons, the two-stage plating may be
attributed to an intrinsic characteristic of Zn deposition. As a typical hexagonal close-
packed metallic material, the initial Zn nucleation favors the formation of
thermodynamically stable crystallites with well-defined shapes, which matches the
thermodynamic Wulff construction. This aligns with our observation that Zn deposits
initially appear in a lumpy morphology. As the plating capacity increases, the lumpy
Zn gradually grows, exposing the highly active Zn(100) and Zn(101) crystal facets
(Figs. 2a, b). As is widely accepted, Zn(100) and Zn(101) facets have a more uneven
equipotential surface along the horizontal direction than that of the Zn(002) facets
(Adv. Mater., 2021, 33: 2100187), which leads to the formation of surface protrusions.
These protrusions typically exhibit concentrated electric fields and high current
densities, serving as deposition hotspots that trigger Zn whisker formation. Once
formed, these whiskers further exacerbate the unevenness of the electric field on the
zinc anode surface, which further results in the rapid growth of mossy Zn. This aligns
well with in-situ optical observations, SEM, and XRD results.

General response: We sincerely thank Reviewer #3 for taking his/her time to review
our work. We understand the reviewer’s concerns regarding the novelty of our study
and would like to take this opportunity to clarify the key advancements and unique
contributions of our work as follows.
Firstly, the formation of electrochemically inactive “dead Zn” is a well-known yet
poorly understood failure mode in Zn batteries. Prior research often attributed it to
passive layer formation or simple dendritic growth. Our work provides clear and
direct evidence that dead Zn originates from a universal two-stage Zn planting and
stripping process. Stage 1 (Lumpy Zn): Initial deposition forms relatively dense,
crystalline Zn deposits, which are often electrochemically reversible. Stage 2 (Mossy
Zn): Subsequent growth occurs preferentially on the protrusions of the lumpy Zn,
forming a porous mossy structure. It is this mossy Zn that, during stripping, loses
electrical contact with the substrate and becomes permanently inactivated as dead Zn.
The discovery of a universal two-stage plating/stripping mechanism that
fundamentally explains the origin of dead Zn formation, a long-standing capacity loss
mechanism in Zn batteries that was previously insufficiently understood.
combination of cationic and anionic reagents to revive the dead Zn. The cations form
a dynamic, positively charged inert region at the Zn/electrolyte interface to disperse
the Zn-ion flux, thereby proactively suppressing the initiation of mossy Zn at the
edges of lumpy Zn deposits. The iodide anions function as a redox mediator. During
charging, it is partly oxidized to I ⁻, which then spontaneously and selectively reacts
3
with the already-formed dead Zn, recycling lost capacity and converting it back to
electroactive Zn2+ for use in the subsequent cycle. As a result, a single-layer Zn//I
2
pouch cell remained a high capacity of ~245.0 mAh after 2500 cycles. In addition, a
practical Ah-scale Zn//I pouch cell showed an outstanding cycling stability for 800
2
cycles with a high-capacity retention of 96.2%, which is at the advanced level of Zn-
metal batteries.
Moreover, we have carefully considered each of concerns and have conducted
extensive new experiments, calculations, and analyses, which were detailed in the
following point by point response. We hope that these revisions resolve all the

Finally, given the novel insights and record-breaking performance metrics, we
respectfully request the reviewer to reconsider the significance and novelty of our
work. We believe this study not only expands the fundamental understanding of Zn
deposition and dead Zn formation, but also provides an effective strategy for practical
aqueous Zn-based batteries, well aligning with the high standards and broad scope of

Response: We thank the reviewer for these critical questions regarding the
universality of the two-stage plating and stripping of the Zn anode. We apologize for
any misunderstanding arising from our original manuscript; it was not our intention to
imply that this behavior is exclusive to the optical cell. On the contrary, our

intrinsic characteristic of Zn electrodeposition, which is retained under certain applied

We fully agree with the reviewer that practical battery systems operate under pressure.
Following the suggestion, we conducted dedicated experiments to investigate the Zn
deposition behavior in coin cells under typical assembly pressures. We disassembled
coin cells after different plating and stripping times at 1 mA cm⁻² and examined the
anode surfaces by optical microscope. As shown in the new Supplementary Fig. 10,
after 10 min of plating, a metallic-luster Zn deposit, i.e., lumpy Zn, appeared on the Ti
surface. As the plating time was increased to 30 min, some black Zn deposits
nucleated on the surface of the lumpy Zn, indicating that mossy Zn began to nucleate
at this stage. When the plating time reached 60 min, the Ti surface was basically
covered by mossy Zn, indicating that mossy Zn would dominate the plating process.
During the subsequent stripping process, the mossy Zn rapidly shrank until only black
insoluble residues were left on the surface of the lumpy Zn which then to dissolve.
The voltage versus time profile is consistent with that of the optical cell. Therefore, it
can be concluded that the Zn plating-stripping behavior still exhibits a two-stage
characteristic even in a pressure-applied coin cell system. It is noteworthy that
pressure does have an obvious effect on the stacked morphology of Zn deposits, as
has been reported in many reports (Adv. Energy Mater., 2023, 14: 2303047; Small,
2025, 21: e2501242). We compared the surface roughness of Zn deposits formed in
coin cells with and without applied stack pressure. As shown in Response Fig. 3, the
27
maximum height difference was reduced from ~242.9 μm (no applied pressure) to
~58.8 μm (under pressure). This indicates that pressure macroscopically compresses
the Zn deposit, making it relatively denser. Critically, however, this macroscopic
compaction did not alter the fundamental two-stage plating mechanism.
To quantify pressure’s impact on Zn deposition, we investigated Zn morphologies
under 0, 0.5, 2.0, and 5.0 MPa by a pressure setup equipped with a pressure sensor
(new Supplementary Fig. 11). At 0 MPa, typical two-stage plating was detected in
this cell. When a stack pressure of 0.5 MPa was applied, the growth of mossy Zn was
slightly suppressed. When the stack pressure was increased to 2.0 MPa, mossy Zn was
still observed after plating for 30 mins. Even at a high stack pressure of 5.0 MPa, two-
stage plating was maintained and the deposited Zn was relatively uniform. Therefore,
while a higher pressure can somewhat compact the Zn deposits, it does not prevent
the inherent drivers that lead to the initial lumpy growth and the subsequent mossy
transition. It is worth noting that glass fiber separators will be crushed when subjected
to pressures exceeding 5.0 MPa. Through these experiments, it can be concluded that
two-stage plating exists in practical systems and warrants attention.

Comments 4: The overall analysis of the effect of ACI is insufficient to clearly
elucidate the underlying mechanism. The mechanism of ACI is unclear for stabilizing
the Zn metal interface.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this critical comment, which provides us with
the opportunity to elaborate more clearly on the underlying mechanism of the ACI.
Based on our existing data and the new experimental and theoretical evidence added
during revision, we propose a dual-function mechanism for ACI with combined
cationic and anionic components to revive dead Zn and stabilize the Zn interface.
Firstly, to directly decouple the effect of the bi-ionic components, we systematically
compared the Zn deposition morphology in three electrolytes, including 1 M ZnOTF,
ZnOTF + 0.5 M ACI (providing both I⁻ anions and acetylcholine cations). As shown
in the Fig. 1c, Fig. 4a and new Supplementary Fig. 17, the Zn deposits from both the
baseline ZnOTF and the ZnOTF-KI electrolyte are loose and porous. In contrast, only
the ACI-added electrolyte produces compact and uniform Zn deposits. In addition, the
assembled Zn//Ti cell and Zn//Zn cell with the ZnOTF-KI electrolyte short-circuited
after ~142 and ~116 h of cycling, respectively (Response Fig. 1), indicating that
mossy Zn still formed within the cells despite the addition of KI. These results
provide clear evidence that the iodide anions alone cannot control the Zn deposition
36
morphology. The dramatic improvement in Zn deposition morphology is achieved
when the acetylcholine cation is present.
Specially, the cationic component primarily acts to prevent the formation of mossy Zn
by creating a positively charged inert region on the anode surface for Zn-ion
dispersion. As demonstrated by the in-situ EQCM data (new Figs. 3a-3c), when the
potential swept from 0.1 V to −0.4 V (vs. Ag/AgCl), the maximum mass increase was
~7.3 and 3.6 ng in the 0.2 M Na SO and 0.2 M Na SO -NaI, respectively. However,
2 4 2 4
~60.1 ng was detected when the ACI was added. This large increase in mass is mainly
attributed to the adsorption of acetylcholine cations rather than Na+, I−, or H O, which
2
indicates that cations can migrate to and adsorb onto the Zn electrode surface under an
electric field.
To better elucidate the cations mediated Zn anode interface, we supplemented the in-
situ electrochemical Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (in-situ FT-IR) to
monitor the dynamic interfacial evolution at the Zn anode. As shown in the new Fig.
3d, in-situ FT-IR were conducted in a spectra-electrochemical cell, which consisted of
a Zn counter/reference electrode, a Ti mesh working electrode, and a ZnOTF-ACI
electrolyte. Galvanostatic discharge tests were performed, and changes in the
interfacial infrared spectra during the discharge were detected. The collected spectrum
at open-circuit potential was used as the background. As shown in the new Fig. 3e,
the absorption band at ~2,980 cm⁻1 is attributed to the C-H stretching band of the
methyl group in the acetylcholine cations. The intensity of the C-H stretching band
progressively increases during Zn plating, indicating a progressive adsorption process
of cations onto the electrode surface. This is also consistent with the results from the
electrochemical EQCM measurements.
To better illustrate the interfacial interactions between the Zn anode and ACI, we have
supplemented the revised manuscript with DFT calculations (new Supplementary
Fig. 14 and Supplementary Date1). The corresponding computational details have
been added to the Methods section of the revised manuscript. As shown in the new
Fig. 3f, the adsorption energy of the horizontal acetylcholine cations (−3.86 eV) was
37
much higher than that of H O (−0.32 eV), Zn2+ (−1.46 eV), iodide anions (−2.79 eV),
2
and the vertical acetylcholine cations (−3.23 eV). This confirms the preferential and
strong adsorption between the acetylcholine cations and Zn anode, which creates a
positively charged inert layer on the Zn anode to disperse Zn2⁺ ions.
Regarding anions for reviving dead Zn, iodide anions can form a certain amount of
oxidative mediator (I −) during charging. These I − preferentially react with dead Zn to
3 3
form electroactive Zn ions that can return for use in the battery cycle. The preferential
reaction of I − with dead Zn was elaborated and experimentally verified in our
3
response to your next Comment 5. Experimental evidence for iodine’s reactivation of
dead Zn was validated through multiple experiments in the original manuscript,
including immersion tests, XRD analysis, and electrochemical measurements.
In summary, based on the original data supplemented by additional experiments and
theoretical calculations, we now have reason to believe that the underlying
mechanism stabilizing Zn anodes by the ACI has been properly elucidated.

Regarding the reviewer’s comment on the adsorption selectivity of ZOTH to fresh Zn
and dead Zn, it is believed that ZOTH can form on both of them. This is because
dead Zn consists of chemically zero-valent metallic Zn and divalent Zn-ion species
(e.g., ZOTH, ZnO), while fresh Zn is zero-valent metallic Zn. ZOTH might form
more easily on dead Zn compared to fresh Zn. We conducted XRD and XPS tests on
dead Zn and fresh Zn after immersing them in the ZnOTF electrolyte for 5 days (new
both the immersed dead Zn and fresh Zn. The intensity of the ZOTH was slightly
higher on the dead Zn than on the fresh Zn. Furthermore, XPS analysis detected a
higher S and F element content on the surface of the immersed dead Zn, suggesting
that dead Zn is more prone to forming the ZOTH byproduct. Consequently, it can be
concluded that ZOTH by-products form more easily on dead Zn than on fresh Zn.
In summary, the I ⁻-mediated rejuvenation process exhibits a beneficial kinetic
3
selectivity towards inactive species, safeguarding the structural integrity of the bulk
Zn anode while effectively recovering lost capacity.

Comments 6: Significantly, the effect of bi-ionic (ACI) should be more deeply studied
with the mechanism and other types of bi-ionic form analogues should be compared.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable question. Regarding the mechanism
of ACI, we have supplemented new experiments, calculations, and analysis, as
detailed in our response to your comment 4. Following the reviewer’s suggestion that
ACI should be compared with other types of bi-ionic form analogues, we have
evaluated a series of bi-ionic analogues to decouple the contributions of the cations
and anions.
replaced I⁻ anions with other halides such as bromide (Br⁻) and chloride (Cl⁻). As
shown in the new Supplementary Figs. 30, 31, cells with acetylcholine bromide
(ACBr) and acetylcholine chloride (ACCl) generated 0.90 and 1.05 mAh cm⁻2 of dead
Zn in the formation cycle, respectively. In the subsequent cycle, they still produced
0.11 and 0.04 mAh cm⁻2 of dead Zn, corresponding to CEs of 89.2% and 95.8%.
This indicates that Cl⁻ and Br⁻ cannot effectively reactivate dead Zn, which might be
attributed to their high oxidation potential required to form oxidizing mediator. In
addition, the long-term cycling stability of Zn anodes was assessed in ZnOTF-ACCl
and ZnOTF-ACBr electrolytes using Zn//Zn symmetric cells (new Supplementary
Figs. 30, 31). While ACBr and ACCl achieved some improvement in Zn||Zn
symmetric cell cycling over the ZnOTF baseline electrolyte (~1130 h and ~1060 h at
5 mA cm⁻2/5 mAh cm⁻2), they were inferior to that of ACI (>2000 h). This
demonstrates that the cations can suppress the formation of mossy Zn to prevent the
cell from short-circuiting in a short time, and the anions are crucial for achieving
ultra-long life via dead Zn recovery.
Secondly, to elucidate the effect of cations, we kept the I⁻ anions constant and
replaced the acetylcholine cations with other structurally related cations, including
choline (C⁺), butyrylcholine (BC⁺), and acetylthiocholine iodide (ATC+). All I⁻-based
bi-ionic analogues (CI, BCI, ATCI) could reactivate dead Zn to some extent, as
evidenced by a CE value exceeding 100% (new Supplementary Figs. 32-34). This
confirms the primary role of the I⁻ anions in capacity recovery. The stability of Zn
plating/stripping, reflected in the symmetric cell cycling, shows significant
improvement after the addition of I⁻-based bi-ionic analogues (new Supplementary
Figs. 32-34). The cycling life decreased in the order: ACI (~2,000 h) > BCI (~1,860
h) > ATCI (~1,270 h) > ChI (~850 h). This ranking might correlate with the
adsorption energy and spatial configuration of the cations on the Zn surface, which
determines their efficacy in suppressing mossy Zn.

Zn formation, while the anion provides a redox-mediated recovery of dead Zn. We
believe these systematic comparisons provide a deeper mechanistic insight requested
by the reviewer and firmly establish the rationale behind our selection of ACI.
